By consuming one of these around the second hour <note>roughly 8:00 AM</note> and another around the tenth hour <note>roughly 4:00 PM</note>, they will suffer no ill effect from hunger. 

There is another composition of the same kind, which takes a half-sextarius <note>about 0.27 liters</note> of Attic sesame, half that amount of honey, a <term>cotyle</term> <gloss>about 0.25 liters</gloss> of oil, and a <term>choenix</term> <gloss>about 1 liter</gloss> of cleaned sweet almonds. One must dry the sesame and the almonds, then grind and sift them. Next, after peeling the squills <note>sea onions</note> all around, cutting away the roots and leaves, and slicing them into small pieces, it is necessary to pound them in a mortar until they are made perfectly smooth. Then, knead an amount of the crushed squills equal to the portion of honey together with the oil, and by pouring it into a pot and placing it over coals, the ingredients must be stirred here and there with a wooden spatula until everything is mixed. When the mass has become solid, it will be worthwhile to divide it into small morsels; anyone taking one in the morning and another in the evening will have sufficient nourishment. Moreover, this medicine is beneficial for an army, for being sweet, it brings satiety and takes away thirst. We have excerpted these notes from a certain manuscript commentary on the book of Heron <note>Heron of Alexandria</note> in the Vatican Library. We have seen the same composition in Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a Byzantine scholar</note>, in the fifth book of military matters, where he describes other similar things of this kind.

->*From which fruits wines can be made.*<-

### CHAPTER XXI.

Now we shall review the fruits from which wines can be made. First, we will cover those commonly made by the ancestors, though there is a twofold distinction: some are for remedies, with which the books of Physicians are filled, and others are for general use. These are of various and nearly infinite kinds, according to the differences of places and nations; for what is given to one is denied to another. First:

->*Wine from palms*<-

Pliny said that in the East, wine is made from these, and he lists fifty kinds of palms and the different types of wines made from them. Among these, the <term>caryotae</term> <gloss>nut-dates</gloss> are most celebrated, being very rich in juice, from which the primary wines of the East are made. These are harmful to the head, from which the fruit takes its name <note>derived from the Greek *karē*, meaning head, implying they cause headaches</note>.
